01-sensation-&-perception.html.title: 01 Sensation & Perception
01-sensation-&-perception.html.description:
Definition: When a stimulus activates the receptors of a sense organ; awareness of changing conditions.Something that causes a bodily response
Definition: Weakest amount of a stimulus required to produce a sensation
Key fact: Detected 50% of the time Definition: Minimum amount of difference a person can detect between two stimuli
Example: Optometrist testing your vision
The larger/stronger a stimulus, the greater the change needed to notice any difference.Definition: Get used to the level of a sensation and respond only to changes away from it
Survival
Prevent overstimulation
Example: Vision adapts in darker areas
Definition: Tendency to detect the presence of stimuli correctly due to motivation, skill, and competing stimuli
Key argument: Argues against a single threshold Pre-attentive (automatic): Unconscious processing
Attentive (careful attention): Conscious, deliberate focus
Definition: The way we interpret sensations and organize them into meaningful experiences.Examples:
Seeing a car
Hearing a song on the radio
Feeling a desk
Perception is shaped by more than the raw sensory input we receive. It is influenced by:
Needs: When we want something, we are more likely to perceive it
Beliefs and expectations: We tend to notice things that fit what we already believe
Previous experience: Past experience helps us interpret new sensory information
These factors help construct the brain's perception tools, which allow us to make sense of the world quickly and efficiently.The brain automatically tries to organize separate pieces of information into wholes.Five Gestalt Principles:
Proximity: Things that are close together are seen as belonging together
Continuity: The brain prefers smooth, continuous patterns
Similarity: Similar things are grouped together
Simplicity: The brain favors the simplest interpretation possible
Closure: The brain fills in missing information to complete a whole
The ability to distinguish between a figure and its background.Examples in senses other than sight:
Walking into a bakery and smelling cinnamon while filtering out every other smell
Eating a big meal and being able to taste the lemon inside of it Retinal disparity: The difference between the images each eye receives; a binocular cue that helps the brain compute depth (greater disparity = closer object).
Convergence: Eyes turn inward (converge) for near objects; feedback from the eye muscles provides a cue to depth and distance.
Constancy: Perceive objects as stable and unchanging despite changes in viewing angle, distance, or lighting. Common forms include size constancy, shape constancy, and brightness (color) constancy.
Illusions: Perceptions that incorrectly represent physical stimuli; visual illusions reveal how perceptual systems use cues and assumptions, sometimes producing systematic errors.
Notes: The attached slide images illustrate retinal disparity (different images from each eye) and shape/size constancy examples (doors shown from different angles). These visual examples highlight how multiple cues and automatic perceptual rules interact to create our stable sense of the environment.

biofeedback.html.title: Biofeedback
biofeedback.html.description:
Definition: Process of learning to control bodily states using specialized machines that provide real-time information about physiological changesStudy: Teaching muscle relaxation through biofeedback

Measured forehead muscle tension (EMG)
Provided visual feedback
Taught to relax these muscles Success: Significantly reduced tension headaches
Patients learned to control muscle tension
Effects lasted after treatment ended See forehead tension rising → stress response
Try relaxation techniques
See tension drop on display → positive reinforcement
Learn mind-body connection
Apply skill in daily life Awareness: Real-time feedback shows the connection
Control: Discover you can influence physiology
Reinforcement: Success with techniques builds confidence
Generalization: Learned control applies outside lab
Possible Arguments:For:
State of focused, narrowed attention
Different brain wave patterns
Relaxation response distinct from normal waking
Against:
Person remains fully conscious
More like skill-learning than consciousness alteration
Not quite the same as meditation or hypnosis
Conclusion: Arguably yes—it produces sustained physiological changes distinct from normal waking consciousness

occipital-lobe.html.description:
Location: Very back of brain (posterior/occipital pole)Location: First visual processing area (back of occipital lobe)Function: Analyzes basic visual featuresPrinciple: Visual field maps directly onto visual cortexResult: Cortex contains distorted "map" of visual world
Route: Occipital → Temporal lobe
Function: Object identification
Question: "What am I looking at?"
Example: Recognizing a face as your friend Route: Occipital → Parietal lobe
Function: Spatial location and movement
Question: "Where is it / where is it going?"
Example: Tracking a moving car Scotoma: Blind spot in visual field (often triangular)
Loss is retinotopic: Corresponds to location of damage
Rest of vision: Usually preserved Can see all basic features
Cannot recognize what they're looking at
"Visual object agnosia" = see but don't recognize
Damage not to V1 but to connections to temporal lobe Massive bilateral occipital damage
Can lead to complete blindness
Some patients have "blindsight" (detect movement without awareness) Specific regions respond to specific colors
V4 area specialized for color
Color perception involves occipital + temporal processing Usually retinal (cone cells lack pigment)
Rarely due to cortical damage alone Middle temporal area (MT/V5) processes motion
Detects direction and speed
Essential for tracking moving objects Akinetopsia: Motion blindness
Can't see movement (see "snapshots")
Extremely rare with cortical damage
Dangerous (can't judge approaching cars) Occipital lobe hyperactivity
Visual disturbances (zigzag lines, blind spots)
Followed by headache Visual hallucinations
Flashing lights, geometric patterns
Often start in back of visual field

parietal-lobe.html.title: Parietal Lobe
parietal-lobe.html.description:
Location: Top and back of brain (behind frontal, above temporal)Definition: The region of parietal lobe that receives and processes touch sensations
Spatial awareness: Knowing where you are
Navigation: Moving through space
Object location: Judging distances
Depth perception: 3D awareness Mental representation of body position
Where limbs are in space
Continuously updated from proprioceptors Spatial neglect: Ignoring one side of space
Ataxia: Loss of coordination
Constructional apraxia: Can't build/draw
The parietal lobe is a sensory and spatial integration center:
Receives sensory input from thalamus
Processes multiple sensory types simultaneously
Integrates with visual information
Coordinates with motor areas for movement Touch sensations from hand (parietal)
Proprioceptive feedback (parietal)
Spatial location of nose (parietal)
Motor command to move hand (frontal)
Result: Successful coordination

perceptual-development.html.title: Perceptual Development
perceptual-development.html.description:
Research Question: When do babies understand depth perception?
Mother sits on far side of "cliff"
Baby placed on near side
Observer watches baby's response
Does baby crawl across apparent cliff? Around 6 months: Baby develops depth perception
~8 months: Mobile enough to notice/fear
First crawlers: More likely to show fear (understand danger)
Non-crawlers: May not show fear yet (can't move) 0-3 months: Responds to loud sounds
3-6 months: Turns to familiar voices
6-12 months: Recognizes own name
12+ months: Understands simple words 0-3 months: Responds to touch, temperature
3-6 months: Explores with mouth, hands
6-12 months: Discriminates textures (soft, rough) Cognitive development: Understand danger
Motor development: Can move toward danger
Memory development: Remember bad experiences
Pattern recognition: Recognize threatening stimuli Provide safe exploration: Let baby explore safely
Gradual challenges: Introduce novel stimuli gradually
Reassurance: Be present during new experiences
Don't force: Respect baby's developmental readiness Babies around 6-8 months develop fear of heights
Earlier: extra dangerous (no fear restraint)
Later: natural caution helps safety
Still need supervision (fear not foolproof)

personality-assessment-methods.html.title: Personality Assessment Methods
personality-assessment-methods.html.description:
Definition: Tests where individuals interpret ambiguous stimuli, with responses revealing their unconscious personality, conflicts, and thought processes
What we project reveals our mind
Unconscious shows through interpretation
No "right" answer = genuine response
Unique interpretations reveal personality
Stimuli: 10 symmetrical inkblots
Show ambiguous inkblot
Ask: "What might this be?"
Note: What they see, where they see it, what details they use
Repeat with 10 inkblots
Analyze responses Seeing "normal" things = good reality contact
Seeing movement = imagination, creativity
Excessive detail = obsessive thinking
Ignoring color = emotional withdrawal Supporters: Reveals unconscious processes
Critics: Low reliability, subjective scoring, limited predictive validity
Research: Mixed results; not widely validated
Stimuli: 30 ambiguous pictures (usually showing 1-3 people in unclear situation)
Show ambiguous picture
Ask: "Tell a story about this picture"
Prompt for: What's happening? What led to it? What will happen?
Record full story
Analyze themes across stories Themes of failure in stories = achievement anxiety
Lonely characters = isolation concerns
Aggressive scenarios = anger issues Better researched than Rorschach
More interpretable stories (clear content)
Still subjective in scoring
Used clinically but not always validated ✓ Open-ended (can't fake easily)
✓ Reveals unconscious material
✓ Rich qualitative data
✓ Good clinical interview starters ✗ Low test-retest reliability
✗ High scorer subjectivity
✗ Difficult to quantify
✗ Limited predictive validity
✗ No strong empirical support for interpretations Still used clinically
Often combined with other assessments
Better as exploratory than diagnostic tool
More common in therapeutic settings than research

psychoanalytic-personality-theory.html.title: Psychoanalytic Personality Theory
psychoanalytic-personality-theory.html.description:
Founder: Sigmund Freud and Carl JungDefinition: Inherited ideas based on ancestors' experiences that shape one's perception
Inherited patterns: Biological, pre-existing
Activate unconsciously: Without awareness
Guide perception: What we notice, how we interpret
Influence behavior: Automatic responses
Show in dreams: Symbolic representations
Appear in myths: Universal story patterns Integrating different archetypes
Balancing light and shadow
Achieving wholeness (individuation)
Becoming authentic self
Research Question: Can aggression be learned through observation?
Participants: Young children
Condition 1: Watch adult behave aggressively toward doll
Condition 2: Watch adult behave calmly
Control: No observation Adult either punches, kicks, or sits quietly with doll
Child watches (or doesn't)
Child later placed in room with similar doll Observed aggression: Children were MORE aggressive
Specific actions: Imitated exact aggressive behaviors
No aggression condition: Children were calm Observation: Watch behavior
Encoding: Remember it
Reproduction: Try the behavior
Motivation: If rewarded/reinforced, repeat Personality shapes how we see environment
Environment provides models and reinforcement
Behavior reflects personality and changes environment
All three constantly influencing each other ✓ Acknowledges unconscious processes
✓ Emphasizes early experience importance
✓ Considers defense mechanisms
✓ Widely influenced psychology ✗ Difficult to test empirically
✗ Based on clinical cases (biased sample)
✗ Overemphasizes childhood
✗ Limited scientific support
✗ Some concepts outdated Psychoanalytic ideas influential but not dominant
Some concepts validated; others discarded
Defense mechanisms still studied
Unconscious processes confirmed by neuroscience
More emphasis on biology than Freud proposed

sensation-basics.html.title: Sensation Basics
sensation-basics.html.description:
Definition: When a stimulus activates the receptors of a sense organ; awareness of changing conditions.A stimulus is something that causes a bodily response
Stimulus: Physical energy in the environment
Sensation: The conscious experience in the brain
Not all stimuli become sensations — many are filtered out!

sensory-adaptation-&-signal-detection.ht.title: Sensory Adaptation & Signal Detection
sensory-adaptation-&-signal-detection.ht.description:
Definition: Getting used to a constant level of stimulation and only responding to changes away from that baselineDefinition: Our ability to detect stimuli depends on motivation, skill, and competing stimuli — not a fixed threshold
Challenges: The traditional idea of absolute thresholds
Proposes: Detection is influenced by psychological factors, not just sensory ability
Airport Security Screening:
High motivation to catch threats
Competing stimuli (thousands of bags)
Cost of miss >> cost of false alarm
→ Results in lower threshold (more false alarms) Happen unconsciously
Very fast
Don't require effort
Process multiple stimuli in parallel
Example: Noticing your name in a crowded room Require conscious attention
Slower
Require mental effort
Process one thing at a time (mostly)
Example: Reading a difficult textbook passage

sensory-thresholds.html.title: Sensory Thresholds
sensory-thresholds.html.description:
Definition: The weakest amount of a stimulus required to produce a sensation
Detected 50% of the time at threshold
Below threshold: no sensation
Above threshold: sensation guaranteed
Definition: Minimum amount of difference a person can detect between two stimuli
Optometrist tests: Making you choose between slightly different lenses
Restaurant volume: Barely hear when someone turns up music slightly
Weight lifting: Can't tell difference between 100 lb and 101 lb, but can between 100 and 110 lb
"The larger or stronger a stimulus, the greater the change needed to notice any difference"K = ΔI / IWhere:
K = Constant (Weber's constant)
ΔI = Smallest detectable change
I = Original stimulus intensity
We perceive differences proportionally, not absolutely!

sleep-disorders.html.title: Sleep Disorders
sleep-disorders.html.description:
Definition: One or more pauses in breathing or shallow breaths while sleeping
Person stops breathing repeatedly during sleep
Breathing resumes (usually with a gasp or snort)
May wake up partially without realizing Poor sleep quality
Daytime fatigue
Increased risk of heart problems
Can lead to sudden death if untreated Obstructive: Airways collapse during sleep
Central: Brain fails to signal breathing muscles
Complex: Combination of both
Definition: Persistent problems falling asleep and/or staying asleep
Stress and anxiety
Poor sleep habits
Medications
Sleep environment (noise, light, temperature)
Mental health conditions (depression, PTSD)
Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine Daytime fatigue and irritability
Difficulty concentrating
Weakened immune system
Increased accident risk
Long-term health problems
Definition: Chronic, overwhelming daytime drowsiness caused by brain's inability to regulate sleep-wake cycles normally
Uncontrollable sleep attacks during day
Person may fall asleep during normal activities
Not simply tired — overwhelming need to sleep
REM sleep enters earlier than normal
May experience cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion) Brain lacks adequate hypocretin/orexin (neurotransmitter regulating wakefulness)
Often caused by autoimmune condition destroying hypocretin neurons
Genetic component also involved Stimulant medications (modafinil, amphetamines)
Scheduled naps
Lifestyle modifications
Sodium oxybate (for cataplexy)

sleep-stages.html.title: Sleep Stages
sleep-stages.html.description:
Biological clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles over approximately 24 hours
Full cycle: ~90 minutes
Nightly cycles: 4-5 complete cycles
First REM: Short (5-10 min)
Last REM: Long (30-60 min)
Stage IV: Gets progressively shorter throughout night
Experience hypnagogic hallucinations (hallucinations between waking and sleep)
Feeling of falling
Hearing your name called
Sleep starts/jerks
Duration: 5-10 minutes
Bridge between wakefulness and sleep
Light sleep
Still easily awakened
Some muscle twitches
Duration: 20 minutes per cycle
Sleep spindles: Brief bursts of rhythmic brain activity
Lowered body temperature
Heart rate slows
Still responsive to sounds
Duration: Variable
Bridge between light and deep sleep
Starting to enter deep sleep
Harder to wake
Duration: 30 minutes
Deepest sleep stage
Hardest to wake from
Parasomnia occur here: Sleepwalking
Sleep talking
Night terrors
Bedwetting Duration: 15-45 minutes per cycle (gets longer as night progresses)
Vivid dreams and nightmares
Sleep paralysis: Can't move (protective mechanism)
Heart rate and breathing increase
Brain wave activity resembles wakefulness
Body temperature regulation fails (feel hot or cold) Enters first REM approximately 90 minutes into sleep
Returns to Stage II after REM
REM periods become progressively longer
Most vivid, longest dreams in final REM cycles

temporal-lobe.html.title: Temporal Lobe
temporal-lobe.html.description:
Location: Sides of brain, near temples (left and right)
Location: Superior temporal lobe
Function: Processes sound frequencies
Processes: Pitch, volume, tone, speech sounds
Location: Left temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus)Function: Understanding spoken and written language
Hippocampus: Long-term memory formation
Amygdala: Emotional memory
Stores: Autobiographical memories, facts, events Receives: Auditory input from primary auditory cortex
Processes: Meaning of words and sentences
Connects: To Broca's area for language production
Connects: To hippocampus for memory Recognizes emotional meaning of words/tones
Links sounds to emotional memories Inferior temporal regions
Recognizes familiar faces
Damage = prosopagnosia (can't recognize faces) Right temporal lobe for melody
Left temporal for rhythm
Musical memory storage Most common type of focal seizure
May cause: Auditory hallucinations
Déjà vu
Emotional changes

Memory loss is primary symptom
Progressive language comprehension decline

the-nervous-system.html.title: The Nervous System
the-nervous-system.html.description:
Function: Controls and coordinates all bodily functionsComponents:
Brain: Control center for all functions
Spinal Cord: Connects brain to PNS; handles reflex actions
Function: Connects CNS to rest of body via branches of nerves
Controls voluntary movements
Transmits sensory info from skin, muscles, joints Controls involuntary functions
Heart rate, digestion, hormones Activation: Threat or stress
Response: Fight-or-flight
Increases: Heart rate, breathing, blood pressure
Decreases: Digestion, immune response Activation: Safety and calm
Response: Rest-and-digest
Decreases: Heart rate, breathing
Increases: Digestion, immune response Action potentials travel along axon
Very fast transmission
All-or-nothing signal Neurotransmitters cross synaptic gap
Slower than electrical
Can be modulated (amplified or inhibited) Fast, automatic response
Protects from immediate harm
Brain learns after action taken Signal reaches brain
Processing occurs
Voluntary decision made
Action taken
Slower but more flexible

trait-theory.html.title: Trait Theory
trait-theory.html.description:
Core Principle: Personality is best understood as a set of measurable traits; everyone possesses all traits to varying degreesEveryone has:
Some level of extraversion (more or less outgoing)
Some level of conscientiousness (more or less organized)
Some level of agreeableness (more or less sympathetic)
Your unique combination creates your personalityAllport identified over 4,000 trait-related words in English!
Definition: Trait so strong, person is identified with it
Rarity: Very rare
Example: "Machiavellian" (though not from Machiavelli himself)
Effect: Dominates personality entirely Definition: Traits that best describe a person
Number: Usually 5-10 main traits
Example: Honest, responsible, cheerful
Effect: Core to personality Definition: Traits less consistent; show situationally
Context-dependent: Only appear in specific situations
Example: Shy at parties but talkative with close friends
Effect: Less central to personality
"Rate yourself 1-7 on each trait"
Person rates themselves
Scored objectively
Produces numerical scores
Reliable and consistent Others rate the person
Can compare to self-report
Reveals blind spots
More objective perspective ✓ Objective measurement
✓ Scientific approach
✓ Predictive validity
✓ Cross-cultural research
✓ Applied uses (job selection, compatibility) ✗ Oversimplifies personality
✗ Ignores situational factors
✗ Doesn't explain why traits exist
✗ Assumes stability (people change)
✗ Self-report bias (people not always accurate)
✗ Doesn't address motivation, values
✗ Cultural differences in trait expression
Idea: Most important traits are encoded in languageProcess:
Find all personality-describing words in dictionary
Reduce to single traits (synonyms combined)
Ask people to rate themselves
Use statistics to find patterns
Result: Core personality dimensions
Finding: Different researchers found different numbers of core traits
Two factors: Introversion-Extraversion
Five factors: "Big Five" (most popular)
Sixteen factors: Myers-Briggs
Others: 3, 6, 7, 10 factors Match personality traits to job requirements
"This job needs high conscientiousness" Compare couple's traits
Identify potential conflicts Trait extremes suggest personality disorders
High neuroticism → anxiety, depression
Low agreeableness → antagonistic behavior Team composition
Leadership potential
Employee selection

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
